First, simultaneously presenting auditory and visual information led to better generalization to novel category items compared to presenting identical information separately within the same trial. Second, multisensory learning could be considered to be better than, worse than, or comparable to unisensory learning, depending on the metric of learning considered. Together, these findings suggest that the way multisensory information is encountered during training directly impacts learning and that presenting information together results in more flexible representations than presenting it separately. More broadly, these results demonstrate the necessity of investigating multisensory learning to reveal how attention and learning function in more naturalistic learning contexts.

[div-01]

Category learning is a core cognitive process by which individuals learn to organize stimuli into meaningful groups, allowing for generalization from known categories to novel instances (Ashby & Maddox, 2011; Minda et al., 2024). When we learn to categorize information in our environment, we usually do not rely on just one sensory modality. Our knowledge about cats, for example, involves visual appearance, auditory vocalizations, as well as tactile and olfactory experiences. People rely on redundant (e.g., auditory and visual information cuing a /b/ phoneme) and complementary multisensory cues (e.g., visual appearance of a cat and "meow" sound) to learn across the lifespan (Newell et al., 2023; Shams & Seitz, 2008). Despite the importance of multisensory information in everyday categorization, relatively little is known about how people learn multisensory categories as most studies of category learning have focused on learning from a single sense, typically vision (Minda et al., 2024; Richler & Palmeri, 2014).

Beyond relevance to real-world behavior, understanding multisensory learning is also critical because there are reasons to expect that presenting information in multiple modalities may facilitate learning (Mathias & von Kriegstein, 2023; Murray & Shams, 2023). Research in recognition memory demonstrates that merely presenting a congruent, redundant sound alongside an image (e.g., cat + "meow") facilitates later recognition of that image (Soto-Faraco & Spence, 2025). Even pairing arbitrary shapes with redundant sounds can enhance memory for those shapes (Brunel et al., 2013; Lauzon et al., 2022). Similar benefits for multisensory learning have recently been demonstrated in category learning. For example, incidental learning of visual categories (e.g., cartoon frogs) is enhanced when a category-specific auditory cue (e.g., unique 'croak' sound) is presented during training (Broadbent et al., 2020; Broadbent et al., 2019). Similarly, learning of novel auditory speech categories (e.g., Mandarin tones) is enhanced when a category-specific visual cue (e.g., line or hand gesture matching the pitch direction) is presented during training (Zhen et al., 2019). Multisensory training improves generalization to novel unisensory category exemplars (Broadbent et al., 2020), suggesting that this benefit is not simply due to the specific information encountered during learning. However, not all studies demonstrate a benefit for multisensory over unisensory category learning (O'Dowd et al., 2025), suggesting the need to understand what underlies multisensory benefits in learning.

One possible explanation for why multisensory training improves learning when it does is that multisensory information enhances perceptual processing by boosting low-level multisensory integration mechanisms that bind cues together into an integrated percept during learning (Murray & Shams, 2023; Stein & Stanford, 2008). However, an alternative explanation is that improved performance is not specific to multisensory processing but instead stems from presenting more variable information during encoding (Broadbent et al., 2020; Hendriks et al., 2023). That is, when people have access to more variable information during learning, regardless of whether information comes from one or multiple modalities, learning is enhanced (Broadbent et al., 2020; Hendriks et al., 2023).

In prior work, information presented in the second modality is often completely task irrelevant. As a result, it remains unclear how people process and learn from information in different modalities when the target of learning itself is multisensory. This is a particularly relevant problem for categorization where information from multiple modalities can be used to determine the category identity -like hearing the song and seeing appearance of a bird to tell its species or combining visual and tactile information to determine an object's identity. In the current study, we address two research questions to understand (1) how multisensory learning is impacted by the way information is presented across modalities and (2) how multisensory learning differs from unisensory learning.

To address the first question, across three experiments, we compare learning of multisensory (audiovisual) categories when learners encounter identical information simultaneously or separately across modalities within a trial. When encountering information simultaneously, learners must process and encode information across modalities at the same time, which also enables multisensory integration due to the temporal coherence of the signals (Stein & Stanford, 2008). When encountering information separately, learners process and encode information in a unisensory context and then can combine information across modalities to make a categorization decision. Critically, in both cases, the categories themselves are multisensory, and learners encounter identical multisensory regularities within and across trials, only differing in how that information is delivered.

We test three competing hypotheses about how simultaneous and separate presentation may impact learning. First, if multisensory learning benefits are driven by multisensory integration supporting enhanced perceptual processing, then learning should be enhanced when auditory and visual information is presented simultaneously compared to separately. This result would not be consistent with an encoding variability account (i.e., Hendriks et al., 2023) because the variability in stimulus information is the same, it only differs in how it is presented. Second, rather than making processing more efficient, presenting multiple pieces of information simultaneously may impair attention, specifically impacting learners' ability to find and use relevant information to make decisions compared to presenting the same information separately when both modalities are given dedicated processing time. As a result, simultaneous presentation may impair learning over separate. Finally, because the amount of information is the same in these two contexts, aligning with the encoding variability account, there may be no differences between simultaneous and separate presentation.

To address the second question, in Experiment 3, we directly compare learning in multisensory and completely unisensory contexts to test four alternative hypotheses. First, multisensory information may facilitate learning over unisensory regardless of how that information is presented. This would be consistent with an encoding variability perspective as there is more information in both multisensory learning contexts to support performance compared to unisensory (Hendriks et al., 2023; Broadbent et al., 2020). Second, multisensory information may facilitate learning over unisensory only when information is presented simultaneously. This would be consistent with a multisensory integration perspective as efficient integration only occurs when information is temporally aligned (Meredith et al., 1987; Stein & Stanford, 2008). Third, if multisensory information in either format poses attentional costs compared to unisensory information (Li & Deng, 2024; Rau et al., 2020; Sandhu & Dyson, 2016), multisensory information may impair learning over unisensory. Finally, it is also possible that multisensory learning may not differ from unisensory, with learners able to extract categoryrelevant information regardless of the context in which it is presented (O'Dowd et al., 2024).

To anticipate, across three experiments, we find that simultaneous presentation consistently facilitates generalization to novel category exemplars relative to separate presentation of the same information, supporting a multisensory integration account of learning benefits. Further, we find that multisensory training can lead to better, worse, or comparable outcomes as unisensory training depending on what aspect of learning is considered. Together, these results suggest that multisensory training impacts how learners attend to and learn from category information.

Experiment 1 Method Participants Participants were 54 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-22 (16 Men, 38 Women) who participated for partial course credit. All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions that varied in how multisensory category information was presented during training (Simultaneous [10 Men, 17 Women], Separate [6 Men, 21 Women]). All participants completed an identical generalization test after training. Participants completed the study in person using the Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). All procedures were approved by the IRB at anonymized for review.

Stimuli

All participants learned two multisensory categories comprised of redundant visual and auditory stimuli. The categories and stimuli for training were identical to a previous study comparing auditory and visual unisensory learning (Roark et al., 2021). Auditory stimuli were 1 sec complex nonspeech ripple sounds varying in temporal (Hz) and spectral modulation (cycles/octave). Visual stimuli were circular Gabor patches presented on a grey background and varying in spatial frequency (cycles/pixel) and orientation (degrees). Category distributions were created sampling from a bivariate Gaussian distribution in normalized space and were then transformed into auditory and visual stimulus spaces (Figure 1A-B). Categories were redundant such that they could be distinguished with a unidimensional rule using information in either modality -spatial frequency dimension of the Gabor patches (rule boundary at 0.05 cycles/pixel) or the temporal modulation rate of the ripple sounds (rule boundary at 7.5 Hz). Stimuli and Task Procedures Note. A. Colored points represent the training stimuli for the two categories and Xs represent stimuli in the generalization test. B. Example visual stimulus (top) and spectrogram of auditory stimulus (bottom). C. Note that order of presentation of modalities in Separate condition was counterbalanced across trials.

There were 100 visual and 100 auditory stimuli (50 per category) presented in the training phase. A separate set of auditory and visual stimuli were created for the generalization test including both near transfer stimuli sampled in an 8x8 grid in the same space as training stimuli (Xs in Figure 1A; 64 auditory, 64 visual) and far transfer stimuli that were shifted along the category-irrelevant dimensions to test the ability to generalize to dissimilar stimuli from training (spectral modulation: near M = 0.86 cycles per octave, far M = -2.94 cycles per octave; orientation: near M = 54.0 degrees, far M = 109.2 degrees; 64 auditory, 64 visual).

Procedure

The procedure included both training (200 trials across 8 blocks of 25 trials) and test phases (112 trials across 4 blocks of 28 trials). Auditory stimuli were presented through Sennheiser over-ear headphones. Auditory and visual stimuli were presented at the same time in the Simultaneous condition and separately within the same trial in the Separate condition (with modality order counterbalanced across trials; Figure 1C). Stimuli in both conditions were presented for 1 sec. To avoid the possible perception of the separately presented auditory and visual stimuli as overlapping due to persistence of stimulus information during the presentation of the second stimulus, Separate trials included a 150 ms interstimulus interval (Bowling & Lovegrove, 1980; Efron, 1970a Efron, , 1970b)). After stimulus presentation, participants were prompted to respond which category the audiovisual stimuli belonged to by pressing the 1 or 2 keys on the keyboard. The assignment of keys to different categories was counterbalanced across participants. Participants had an unlimited amount of time to respond. Immediately after their response, participants received feedback (Correct or Incorrect) for 1 sec, followed by a 1 sec inter-trial interval.

In the test phase, participants categorized auditory-only ( 16 trials

Results

Accuracy improved across training (block 1: M = 65%, block 8: M = 81%; p < .0001), indicating successful learning (Figure 2A; F(7, 364) = 16.8, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.11). Training accuracy did not differ across Simultaneous (M = 74%) and Separate conditions (M = 79%; F(1, 52) = 2.77, p = .10, ηG² = 0.032) and condition did not interact with block (F(7, 364) = 1.93, p = .064, ηG² = 0.014). Note. Error bars represent SEM. Horizontal line at 50% represents chance-level performance in left and center panels. Horizontal line at 0.50 represents responses aligning with neither modality in right panels.

In contrast to training, generalization test accuracy was significantly higher in the Simultaneous (M = 71%) than Separate condition (M = 62%; F(1, 52) = 7.065, p = .010, ηG² = 0.075). Accuracy also differed across trial types (F(2, 104) = 9.21, p = .00021, ηG² = 0.037), with a significant interaction between condition and trial type (Figure 2B; F(2, 104) = 4.55, p = .013, ηG² = 0.019) which we investigate further with Bonferroni-corrected comparisons.

Performance in the Simultaneous condition was significantly better than the Separate condition for auditory-only (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001) and audiovisual trials (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001), and conditions did not differ on visual-only trials (Mdifference = 3%, p = .26). For the Simultaneous condition, test performance was worse when only visual information was presented (M = 64%) compared to when only auditory (M = 73%; p = .0020) or audiovisual information was presented (M = 76%; p < .0001). Auditory only and audiovisual trials did not differ (p = .41). In contrast, for the Separate condition, performance did not differ across trial types (audiovisual: M = 63%, auditory: M = 61%, visual: M = 61%, ps > .51).

Conditions also differed in how they responded to incongruent auditory and visual information. While responses in the Simultaneous condition were more strongly aligned with the auditory than visual modality (Figure 2C; M = 0.64; t(26) = 3.82, p = .00074, d = 0.74), responses in the Separate condition did not clearly align with either modality (M = 0.57; t(26) = 1.85, p = .075, d = 0.36). Though the conditions demonstrated different patterns, the conditions were not significantly different (M = 0.07; t(51.9) = 1.30, p = .20, d = 0.35).

Discussion

In Experiment 1, we found that the way identical category information was presented impacted how learners attended to and learned multisensory categories. Specifically, simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization performance than separate, particularly on audiovisual and auditory-only trials. These results support a multisensory integration account of learning benefits, but there are some aspects of our design that prevent us from drawing firm conclusions. We address these aspects in Experiment 2.

Experiment 2 Method

To account for possible alternative explanations for the results in Experiment 1, we made several changes to Experiment 2. First, while stimuli in the two conditions were identical, conditions differed in both how stimuli were presented and the total stimulus duration such that differences could be due to the relatively short time Simultaneous learners had to process the stimuli (1 sec) compared to Separate learners (1 sec + 1 sec = 2 sec). In Experiment 2, we disentangle these explanations by separately manipulating presentation format and stimulus duration. Second, all audiovisual test stimuli were presented simultaneously, potentially introducing an unintended familiarity benefit in the Simultaneous condition. In Experiment 2, we counterbalance the presentation and duration of test trials to not unfairly advantage any condition. Third, while the pattern of responses for incongruent stimuli was qualitatively different in the two conditions (d = 0.35), the overall effect was not significant. Given the observed effect size, we were underpowered to observe a difference (sensitivity analysis indicated that our sample size could detect an effect of d = 0.78 or larger with 80% power). In Experiment 2, we collect a higher-powered sample given the effect sizes observed in Experiment 1. Finally, we added attention checks throughout training to ensure that participants were attending to both modalities throughout the task. Experiment 2 was pre-registered and we report all planned confirmatory analyses (https://osf.io/meuyh/overview?view_only=a029de89132248439c6c35b4968a0bed).

Participants

Participants were 132 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-26 ( 20Men, 112 Women) who completed the study in person for partial course credit. Participants all reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (Short [1 sec], Long [2 sec]): Simultaneous-Long (N = 34; 7 Men, 27 Women), Simultaneous-Short (N = 31; 5 Men, 26 Women), Separate-Long (N = 33; 5 Men, 28 Women), Separate-Short (N = 34; 3 Men, 31 Women). According to the power analysis outlined in the preregistration, our final sample had 132 participants after exclusion of 56 participants due to failure of auditory and visual attention checks (< 85% accuracy on both types).

Stimuli

Experiment 2 included the same training stimuli and the near transfer test stimuli from Experiment 1. Auditory stimuli durations were 0.5, 1, or 2 sec depending on condition.

Procedure

The training procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that conditions also varied in the total stimulus duration -relatively Short (Separate: 0.5 sec + 0.5 sec; Simultaneous: 1 sec) or Long (Separate: 1 sec + 1 sec; Simultaneous: 2 sec). Simultaneous-Short and Separate-Long conditions are identical to the conditions from Experiment 1. Additionally, attention check trials occurred five times each in every training block and required pressing the spacebar within 2 sec after hearing a 2 sec 1000 Hz pure tone or seeing a visual cue to press the spacebar. The test procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that participants completed more trials overall (auditory-only: N = 32, visual-only; N = 32, audiovisual congruent: N = 32, audiovisual incongruent: N = 32), only near transfer stimuli were used, and presentation and duration were counterbalanced across trials. At the end of the experiment, as exploratory measures, participants were asked how they used modality information to make decisions during learning and whether they thought the modalities were related to each other (see Supplemental Materials).

Results

Accuracy improved across training, indicating successful learning (Figure 2D; F(7, 896) = 35.3, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.098; block 1: M = 63%; block 8: M = 78%, p < .0001). As in Experiment 1, training accuracy did not differ across Simultaneous (M = 74%) and Separate conditions (M = 73%; F(1, 128) = 0.29, p = .59, ηG² = 0.001). Training accuracy was better when stimuli were presented for relatively long (M = 77%) compared to short durations (M = 71%; F(1, 128) = 6.14, p = .015, ηG² = 0.028). There were no significant interactions (ps > .11).

As in Experiment 1, generalization test accuracy was significantly higher in the Simultaneous (M = 76%) than Separate condition (M = 64%; F(1,128) = 33.9, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.15). Accuracy also differed across trial types (Figure 2E; F(2, 256) = 45.4, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.10) such that accuracy was highest for audiovisual trials (M = 75%), followed by auditory-only (M = 71%), and then visual-only trials (M = 63%; ps < .0001). In contrast to Experiment 1, there was no interaction between training condition and trial type (F(2, 256) = 0.45, p = .64, ηG² = 0.001). Test accuracy did not differ across duration conditions (F(1, 128) = 1.97, p = .16, ηG² = 0.010) and there were no other interactions (ps > .21).

As a planned exploratory analysis, we examined the effect of test trial type separating the two audiovisual trial types (separate, simultaneous). As in Experiment 1, there was a significant interaction between training condition and test trial type (F(3, 384) = 2.99, p = .031, ηG² = 0.0080).

Performance in the Simultaneous condition was significantly better than the Separate condition across all trial types (ps < .00047). Surprisingly, performance was 10% better in the Simultaneous condition (M = 82%) for audiovisual-separate trials that exactly matched the training format for the Separate condition (M = 72%). To contextualize this surprising finding, we conducted an additional exploratory analysis comparing accuracy in the final training block with the two types of audiovisual test trials in the two conditions. There was a significant interaction between training condition and trial type (F(2, 256) = 24.7, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.067).

Participants in the Simultaneous condition seamlessly transferred their knowledge from the final training block to the audiovisual test trials (block 8: 77%, test-separate: 82%, test-simultaneous: 82%; ps > .18). In contrast, in the Separate condition, accuracy for both types of audiovisual test trials was significantly worse than the final training block (block 8: 80%, test-separate: 72%, test-simultaneous: 65%; ps < .020).

For the Simultaneous condition, performance did not differ across audiovisual test trials that presented information separately (M = 82%) or simultaneously across modalities (M = 82%; p = 1.0), but performance was impaired when information in only one modality was presented (visual: M = 69%, auditory: M = 77%) compared to both audiovisual test trial types (ps < .017).

For the Separate condition, performance was significantly better for audiovisual test trials that matched their training format (M = 72%) compared to when information was presented simultaneously (M = 65%, p = .030). Performance was impaired when only visual information was presented (M = 58%) compared to both audiovisual test trial types (ps < .031) but was only impaired when auditory information was presented (M = 64%) compared to audiovisual-separate trials (p = .00075; auditory-only vs. audiovisual-simultaneous: p = 1.0).

Returning to the planned confirmatory analyses, as in Experiment 1, conditions differed in how they responded to incongruent auditory and visual information (Figure 2F). While responses in the Simultaneous conditions were more strongly aligned with the auditory than visual modality (Short: M = 0.68, t(30) = 5.53, p < .0001, d = 0.99; Long: M = 0.63; t(33) = 3.05, p = .0045, d = 0.52), responses in the Separate conditions did not clearly align with either modality (Short: M = 0.59; t(33) = 2.72, p = .010, d = 0.47; Long: M = 0.56; t(32) = 1.84, p = .076, d = 0.32). In contrast to Experiment 1, in this higher-powered study, responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli significantly differed across conditions (F(1, 128) = 5.78, p = .018, ηG² = 0.043) -responses were more strongly aligned with the auditory modality after Simultaneous (M = 0.66) than Separate training (M = 0.57). Responses did not differ across training duration (F(1,128) = 1.28, p = .26, ηG² = 0.10) or the interaction between presentation and duration (F(1,128) = 0.18, p = .67, ηG² = 0.001).

Discussion

Experiment 2 replicated the effects of Experiment 1 while also controlling for potential confounds. In Experiment 2, simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization performance than separate for all trial types and encouraged learners to rely more on auditory than visual information. These results support a multisensory integration account of learning benefits as learning was enhanced when identical information was presented simultaneously.

Critically, it remains unclear how these multisensory conditions compare to unisensory learning.

We address this directly in Experiment 3.

Experiment 3

In Experiment 3, we replicate comparisons of Separate and Simultaneous training in a broader participant sample collected online and directly compare multisensory to unisensory training. To simplify comparisons and because duration did not impact test performance, total stimulus duration was held constant across conditions (2 sec). Experiment 3 was pre-registered and we report all planned confirmatory analyses (https://osf.io/ugp34/overview?view_only=4d1dc6d0812d40398617d3027ce21725).

Method

Participants

Participants were 180 adults recruited online from Prolific ages 18-64 (95 Men, 85 Women) who completed the study online for a small payment ($10). Participants all reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate, Unisensory). There were 55 participants in the Simultaneous condition (18-53 years, 30 Men, 25 Women), 56 participants in the Separate condition (18-64 years, 29 Men, 27 Women), and 69 participants in the Unisensory condition (18-62 years, 36 Men, 33 Women). Per the power analysis outlined in the pre-registration, our final sample had 180 participants after exclusion of 37 participants due to failure of auditory and/or visual attention checks.

Stimuli

Stimuli were identical to Experiment 2. Stimuli were presented for relatively long durations with a total stimulus duration of 2 sec.

Procedure

The training procedures for the Simultaneous and Separate conditions were identical to the long duration conditions from Experiment 2. In the Unisensory condition, participants only encountered information in one modality, with the trained modality (auditory, visual) counterbalanced across participants. The same attention checks were used as Experiment 2.

Unisensory condition attention checks were only given in the trained modality. All participants completed the same test procedure as Experiment 2 with auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisualseparate, and audiovisual-simultaneous trial types. In the Unisensory conditions, test performance in the untrained modality was significantly but weakly better than chance (M = 56%, t(68) = 3.90, p < .0001, d = 0.47), but training performance did not significantly differ across auditory and visual modalities (t(61.9) = 1.26, p = .21, d = 0.30). Participants completed the same exploratory questionnaire measures as Experiment 2 (see Supplementary Materials).

Results

Accuracy improved across training, indicating successful learning (Figure 2G; F(7, 1239) = 37.79, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.083; block 1: M = 65%; block 8: M = 80%, p < .0001). Training accuracy differed across conditions (F(2, 177) = 6.61, p = .0020, ηG² = 0.041) such that accuracy was higher in the Separate (M = 80%) than Unisensory condition (M = 72%, p = .0012), with no differences between Simultaneous and other conditions (M = 75%, ps < .086). Condition did not interact with block (F(14, 1239) = 0.54, p = .91, ηG² = 0.003).

Overall test performance differed across conditions (F(2, 177) = 4.34, p = .014, ηG² = 0.47). As in prior experiments, generalization test accuracy was significantly higher in the Simultaneous (M = 75%) than Separate condition (M = 69%, p = .030). Simultaneous multisensory learning resulted in better test performance than Unisensory learning (M = 69%, p = .036), while Separate multisensory learning was comparable to Unisensory (p = 1.0). However, these results were driven by differences in the untrained modality. When removing untrained modality trials, conditions still differed (F(2, 177) = 4.30, p = .015, ηG² = 0.046), but test performance was comparable in Simultaneous (M = 75%) and Unisensory conditions (M = 76%, p = 1.0) and worse in Separate (M = 69%) than the Unisensory condition (p = .021).

To investigate the impact of test trial type and the interaction with condition, we slightly deviated from our planned analysis to enable treating test trial type as a fully within-subjects variable -instead of collapsing across Unisensory conditions, we examined auditory and visual Unisensory conditions separately. As in previous experiments, accuracy differed across trial types (Figure 2H; F(3, 528) = 34.0, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.066) and this effect significantly interacted with condition (F(9, 528) = 16.9, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.095).

In examining how presentation format impacts multisensory learning, we found that performance was significantly better in the Simultaneous than Separate conditions, but this pattern was only significant for visual-only trials (Mdifference = 8%, p = .040), with no differences in other trial types after correcting for multiple comparisons (auditory-only: Mdifference = 5%, p = .38; audiovisual-simultaneous: Mdifference = 8%, p = .12; audiovisual-separate: Mdifference = 5%, p = .96).

In comparing unisensory and multisensory learning, we found that effects depended on trial type. When training was unisensory or multisensory, performance did not differ across auditory-only (Unisensory-auditory: M =74%; Separate: 73%, p = 1.0; Simultaneous: M = 78%; p = .96) or audiovisual trials (ps > .14) but performance was much better in visual-only trials when training was unisensory (Unisensory-visual: M = 79%; Separate: M = 59%, p < .0001; Simultaneous: M = 67%, p = .0044).

When participants learned Unisensory categories, they successfully generalized to both unisensory and multisensory stimuli. Performance on trained-modality trials (auditory: M = 74%; visual = M = 79%) was not different from audiovisual trials (auditory: separate: M = 73% vs. simultaneous: M = 76%; visual: separate: M = 76% vs. simultaneous: M = 77%; ps > .99).

Different from Experiment 2, when participants learned multisensory categories either Separately or Simultaneously, learning similarly generalized to audiovisual trials that matched or were different from the training format for both Simultaneous (separate: 81% vs. simultaneous: 81%, p = 1.0) and Separate conditions (separate M = 76% vs. simultaneous: M = 73%, p = .48). In both conditions, performance also did not differ across auditory-only and audiovisual trials (Separate: M = 73%, ps > .50; Simultaneous: M = 78%, ps > .70), but performance was significantly worse on visual-only trials than all other trial types (Separate: M = 59%, ps < .0001; Simultaneous: M = 67%, ps < .00058).

Next, we examined accuracy across the final training block and audiovisual test trials (collapsing across Unisensory conditions as planned). As in Experiment 2, there was a significant interaction between condition and trial type (F(4, 354) = 7.68, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.025).

Participants seamlessly transferred their knowledge from training to test in both Simultaneous (block 8: 80%, test-separate: 81%, test-simultaneous: 81%; ps > .99) and Unisensory conditions (block 8: 75%, test-separate: 75%, test-simultaneous: 76%; ps > .99). In contrast, just as in Experiment 2, when information was presented Separately during training, accuracy for both types of audiovisual test trials was significantly worse than the final training block (block 8: 85%, test-separate: 76%, test-simultaneous: 73%; ps < .00093).

Finally, we examined how participants responded to incongruent auditory and visual information (Figure 2I). We deviated slightly from our pre-registered plan to enable more interpretable comparisons across conditions -we did not collapse Unisensory conditions and compared all conditions on the same measure, alignment with the auditory modality. Conditions differed in how they responded to incongruent stimuli (F(3, 176) = 36.5, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.38).

When participants were trained on the visual modality, responses were aligned more with the visual than auditory modality (M = 0.28, t(36) = -8.02, p < .0001, d = -1.32) which was significantly different from all other conditions (ps < .0001). When participants were trained on the auditory modality (M = 0.67, t(31) = 5.65, p < .0001, d = 1.00) or both modalities Separately (M = 0.62, t(55) = 4.16, p = .00011, d = 0.56) or Simultaneously (M = 0.70, t(54) = 6.79, p < .0001, d = 0.92), responses were aligned more with the auditory than visual modality and this did not differ across conditions (ps > .34). This suggests that multisensory training -Separate or Simultaneous -encourages attention to the auditory over the visual modality, resulting in impaired visual-only test performance.

Discussion

In Experiment 3, we replicated a core finding from Experiment 2 in a broader sample of participants who completed the tasks online -multisensory learning with simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization to novel exemplars than separate presentation.

However, rather than an across-the-board benefit, the benefit was restricted to visual-only trials and better preservation of performance from training to test. Inclusion of unisensory conditions further clarified the locus of these benefits. Multisensory training did not uniformly enhance learning over unisensory -performance was comparable, better, or worse in unisensory contexts depending on the type of information being categorized.

General Discussion

Across three experiments, we found that simultaneous presentation of redundant auditory and visual category information resulted in better test performance than when the same information was presented separately. We also found that multisensory learning resulted in comparable, better, or worse outcomes than unisensory learning depending on the information available in the test. These results suggest that multisensory learning can introduce both costs and benefits as learners prioritize information in one modality over the other. The benefits are higher and costs lower when multisensory information is presented simultaneously rather than separately.

Simultaneous Presentation is Better than Separate for Multisensory Learning

All experiments demonstrated that Simultaneous presentation led to better test outcomes than Separate, though the nature of the benefits differed somewhat across experiments. In general, these results support a multisensory integration perspective, such that synchronous multisensory signals are integrated in low-level perceptual processing (Meredith et al., 1987; Stein & Stanford, 2008), so receiving the same information simultaneously is more advantageous than receiving it separately. This result does not support the explanation that learning benefits from higher encoding variability because the information was identical, only varying in how it was presented within a trial. We next address other potential explanations for the benefits of simultaneous over separate multisensory learning.

Our results also suggest a distinction between learning (i.e., performance in training) and outcomes of learning (i.e., performance in generalization test). While the conditions did not differ in performance during training, Simultaneous training facilitated generalization performance over Separate. These different patterns in training and test are due to preservation of performance in the Simultaneous condition and deterioration in the Separate condition. In the test, participants no longer received feedback and encountered unisensory stimuli and audiovisual stimuli presented differently than what they encountered during training. One possible explanation for these results is that Separate presentation may have increased the cognitive load of the task. Because information was presented separately in time, participants may have intentionally held information about the first stimulus in working memory while processing the second stimulus, which could have impaired learning (Miles & Minda, 2011; Zeithamova & Maddox, 2006). While this did not disrupt performance during training, by engaging these resources, participants may have become more fatigued, impairing performance on the final task of the experiment (i.e., generalization test). Further, because we counterbalanced the order of auditory and visual stimuli across trials, participants may have subjectively experienced different trials as switching between different tasks, which may have added additional cognitive load that could have impaired learning (Dubravac et al., 2026; Erickson, 2008; Roark, 2025). To explore this possibility, we compared the time it took participants to complete the tasks with the assumption that taking longer would be associated with additional cognitive demand and fatigue (Chen et al., 2011). It took participants significantly longer to complete the Separate (M = 23.3 minutes) than Simultaneous condition (M = 20.5 minutes, t(47.1) = 2.92, p = .0053, d = 0.80), but only in Experiment 1. There were no differences in completion time across conditions in Experiments 2 or 3 (see Supplemental Materials). This does not eliminate the possibility of differences in cognitive load across conditions, but it does not strongly support it either.

The persistent deterioration in performance from training to test may also suggest that Separate learners are particularly sensitive to changes in how information is presented because of how they expect information to unfold over time. In the test, when one modality was presented, it may or may not have been followed by a second modality. Because Separate learners were used to receiving information in one modality and then the other, when information in the relatively weak visual modality was presented, learners may have expected auditory to follow it and when it did not come, they could not retroactively change how they attended to visual information to make an accurate decision. Thus, this resulted in impaired performance on visual-only trials compared to audiovisual-separate trials. Similarly, in the test, if both modalities were presented simultaneously, Separate learners unaccustomed to encountering information in this way may have been overwhelmed, unable to extract key information to make an accurate decision. While Unisensory learners would simply need to ignore additional apparently irrelevant modality information, Separate learners may expect the information to come separately with dedicated processing time and now must process the same information rapidly together. Thus, audiovisualsimultaneous trials have increased attentional costs compared to audiovisual-separate because the presentation format violated their expectations. Though this detriment in audiovisualsimultaneous trials for Separate relative to Simultaneous training was statistically significant in Experiments 1 (-12%) and 2 (-17%), the pattern was present (-8%) but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons in Experiment 3. However, this pattern suggests a potential benefit for Simultaneous learning in that it may result in more flexible attention when learners encounter information in different formats than training. It is possible that providing information about which modality or modalities will be presented on the upcoming trial or informing learners during learning that they would later encounter information in different formats might enable Separate learners to overcome this impairment if it is due to violations of expectations. This remains a topic for future work.

Costs and Benefits to Multisensory Learning

We found that multisensory learning was comparable, better, and worse than unisensory learning depending on how learning was defined. This indicates that understanding the potential costs and benefits to multisensory over unisensory learning requires defining the target of learning. If the target of learning is performance on both modalities individually and together, simultaneous multisensory learning is best as it enables the highest accuracy across all kinds of stimuli -auditory, visual, and audiovisual. If the target of learning is performance in one modality, simultaneous multisensory or unisensory learning are preferable to separate multisensory learning as both led to high accuracy on unisensory trials. However, if the target of learning is performance in one specific modality, then unisensory learning is best. While auditory learning was similar in unisensory and multisensory contexts, visual learning was impaired in multisensory contexts as learners prioritized information in the auditory modality.

Our results suggest that presenting information in multiple modalities impacts how learners attend to information during learning. Here, multisensory learning encouraged attention to the auditory modality particularly when information was presented simultaneously. Recall that optimal performance in this task could be achieved by attending to either or both auditory and visual modalities. Thus, it is not inherently surprising that learners primarily made decisions based on only one modality. However, this apparently rational attention strategy came at a cost of impaired visual learning compared to when learning was unisensory.

At first glance, these results seem to conflict with prior work demonstrating that when redundant information across modalities is presented simultaneously, people (especially adults) rely more on the visual modality (Barnhart et al., 2018; Colavita, 1974; Colavita & Weisberg, 1979; Robinson & Sloutsky, 2004). One possible explanation for these differences is that we presented stimuli for relatively short durations (0.5-2 sec). Because auditory information is inherently fleeting, people can successfully process very rapid auditory information (Penney et al., 2000; Shamma, 2001), when information is presented at relatively short durations, auditory learning is often preserved while visual performance is impaired (Emberson et al., 2010) and decisions are less dominated by vision (Ciraolo et al., 2020; Robinson & Sloutsky, 2019). Most studies of visual category learning present the visual stimulus until the participant responds (e.g., Crossley et al., 2025) and when visual information is presented at shorter durations, accuracy tends to be impacted (Roark et al., 2021). Interestingly, varying the duration of stimulus presentation in Experiment 2 did not impact how learners attended to one modality over the other. Future studies should examine performance at longer durations to understand the driving factors of auditory dominance in category learning.

Together, these results suggest that when considering which format is most beneficial for learning, it is essential to understand the intended learning goal. While prior studies of multisensory learning often introduce a second modality as a task-irrelevant feature and do not always assess learning in the second modality, this may limit our understanding of the potential costs and benefits to multisensory learning when the target of learning is inherently multisensory. This is critical as many real-world categories are not simply unisensory categories that may benefit from incidental information in another modality -categories like bird species, rock types, or even speech categories are inherently multisensory. Our results suggest that presenting multisensory information has broader consequences for learning than have previously been considered, particularly in impacting how people attend to information across modalities. Our results expand understanding of multisensory learning by demonstrating that depending on the target of learning and the way information is presented across modalities, multisensory learning can benefit, impair, or be comparable to learning from a single modality. These results also pose significant challenges for current theories of category learning, which do not explicitly account for learning across different sensory modalities.

Figure1 ), visual-only (16 trials), and audiovisual stimuli (48 trials) without feedback.

Most audiovisual trials were congruent (auditory and visual stimuli signal same category identity, N = 32: near transfer: N = 16, far transfer: N = 16) and some were incongruent (auditory and visual stimuli signal different category identities, N = 16, all near transfer). Audiovisual test stimuli were always presented simultaneously in the test. The trial procedure was similar to training except that participants did not receive any feedback. For incongruent audiovisual stimuli, we examined how participants resolved incongruent information by computing the proportion of responses aligned with the category indicated by the auditory stimulus such that values > 0.50 indicate stronger use of auditory information, values < 0.5 indicate stronger use of visual information, and values around 0.50 indicate similar use of both modalities.
